title: Forty Mysteries and a Hotel That Knows My Name
subtitle: Mystery, investigation and classic adventures

opening.title: The Deposit Was Supposed to Be Refundable
paragraphs: “Nigga, why does the sign say intimate?” Tank asked. Behind him, two men were assembling a doorway large enough to admit a modest yacht. A third man held my face. Six feet of it, printed on a board. The face looked confident. That nigga had not seen the invoice.

“Because it's a gathering of close friends.” Tank looked at the ballroom. “How close? We sharing a zip code?” Shawna walked between us with her evening shoes in one hand. She had booked a suite, chosen a dress, and asked for a night where she could actually enjoy her husband. I had interpreted this as a request for three adjoining entertainment spaces and a photographer. My wife loved me deeply. Love sometimes looked like a woman stopping in a doorway to count backward.

The casino hotel called the room Imperial. I had called the party Panorama. Mercedes called it a soundcheck waiting to be interrupted. She was doing a short live set because she wanted to try an arrangement with musicians she trusted. She wanted a recording she controlled, a working monitor, and nobody from the drinks sponsor explaining how to reach a younger audience. Everyone in our party was a grown adult. Several of us had grown much more successfully than I had.

Rosa arrived with the catering supervisor and put a hand against the decorative doorway. “Food goes through here?” I said guests would pass beneath it and feel transported. She asked whether transported guests intended to eat. The doorway moved. Tank helped move it, then came back holding a tiny gold torch from the decoration crate. “What this belong to?” I pointed at a cloth-covered statue. He lifted one corner, stared, and let the cloth fall. “Nigga, we discussing that later.”

I had wanted an evening with games because somebody had asked what might be enjoyable. Mysteries. Interesting people. Places where a person could stop and think. I understood all of that. Unfortunately I also understood champagne towers, hired atmosphere, and the magnificent possibilities of being photographed pointing at something. The people who loved me had arrived to enjoy the first idea and survive the rest.

Shawna slipped her arm through mine. “You remember upstairs?” “Baby, I remember everything.” “You remember the strawberries?” I looked toward the buffet. Her fingers tightened. “The private strawberries, Aiden.” Oh. Those strawberries. I leaned closer and told her I had reserved considerable personal attention for her. She said attention had been reserved all afternoon and was beginning to incur a cancellation fee.

Mercedes came over carrying a black equipment bag. “This stays with me or Porsche. The recorder and spare drive are in here.” I reached to take it. She moved it back. “Are you me or Porsche?” “I'm offering support.” “Offer your elbow to your wife. She looks under-supported.” Shawna accepted the elbow with a smile that made my hotel trousers feel like an ambitious tailoring decision.

Tank's old friend Darnell arrived in a blue jacket and announced that he'd brought enough atmosphere for everybody. Tank looked at the bag, then looked at him. “My nigga, tell me you mean playlists.” Darnell smiled instead of answering. Mercedes pointed him toward the coat room, away from her equipment. We would be learning more about his contribution shortly, which is usually how a sentence about Darnell develops.

The photographer asked me to stand beside the sponsor's banner. I did. The sponsor asked Mercedes to join me holding a bottle. She said she'd be happy to discuss a separate advertising fee. He laughed. She didn't. The photographer lowered his camera and became interested in a light stand. A whole room of professionals suddenly understood that my friend was working, and I was the only nigga dressed like a man receiving a lifetime achievement award for booking chairs.

Shawna took the microphone before I could introduce the evening. “The games are in there. Pick what interests you. The practical notes explain what each one asks. Nobody has to finish anything.” Short. Clear. Completely devastating to my twelve-minute welcome. I asked whether I could add a thought. “At dinner,” she said. “To one person.” Tank put a plate in my free hand. Rosa pointed at the room. Mercedes began testing her microphone. The party started without waiting for my permission, and my face on the big board watched it happen.

games.case_title: The Ghost Doesn't Pay the Resort Fee
scene: I put a second chair beside the screen for Joey Mallone. Blackwell had a woman dealing with a ghost; my hotel had charged me for six hundred people, and I intended to count the dead.
Tank picked up the place card. “Nigga, this seat got a meal?”
“Spiritually.” “Then move your spiritual ass. Rosa made crab cakes.” He sat down and ate Joey's welcome portion before I could establish contact.

Our Rosa watched the game's Rosa talk to somebody nobody else could see. “I like her,” she said. “People keep giving this woman responsibilities she didn't order.” She looked directly at me. I checked behind myself. Nothing there. Expensive habit.
Shawna leaned against my shoulder. “A ghost could walk through our suite door.” “Baby, so could I.” “Last night you walked into it.”
Joey had been dead for years. Nigga still entered a room with more dignity than me.
games.pleasure: A compact New York supernatural mystery joins a reluctant medium to a sardonic spirit guide. Conversations and notebook connections make discovery feel personal; the developing partnership offers more reason to continue than simply clearing another puzzle.
games.burden: Notebook combinations, returning to locations, and remembering names remain real work. Suicide and bereavement are central. Reviews report no timed or dexterity challenges, but this is not a complete-path playtest. Current desktop patches offer manual speech advance through a Ctrl+P toggle; verify it waits.

games.ruling: Try the partnership if it catches you; Joey can handle supernatural business while I handle his crab-cake debt, which Tank insists survives death.
games.source_note: Inspected publisher premise and developer Ctrl+P patch notice; timing description is a secondary review, not current complete-path testing. PC original only.

games.case_title: The Paranormal Department Has My Room Key
scene: Somebody called the ballroom phone and breathed into it. I told security we had a haunting. Mercedes took the receiver, listened, and said, “Tank. Stop eating against the microphone.”
“Nigga, I'm ordering ice.” “You're calling the stage.” “Then send some dramatic ice.”

The Darkside Detective appeared on the monitor while the hotel manager asked why I had requested an exorcist. I pointed at McQueen. “Professional comparison.” He pointed at the charge for an emergency callout. The hotel apparently billed ghosts by the hour.

Shawna tested an inventory movement. I reached over to demonstrate and dragged the wrong thing. She rested her hand on mine. “Help me by stopping.” That felt almost sexual until she moved my whole arm off the table.
Mercedes gave Tank the correct number. He ordered ice, a sandwich, and cancellation of the priest. The sandwich arrived first. Stronger management than mine.
games.pleasure: Comic paranormal investigations offer a recurring detective partnership and short case boundaries. Static scenes let attention settle on objects, dialogue, and absurd situations rather than keeping an avatar and camera moving together.
games.burden: Current Steam metadata declares play without timed input. That does not mean hold-free: PC reviews describe dragging inventory items onto objects or other items. Pipe and tile puzzles also appear. Text reading and small hotspots deserve an actual check before treating this as comfortable.
games.first: Begin the first case, inspect one object, and test one inventory drag. Check that text advance and the save/exit route feel understandable before continuing.
games.ruling: The little cases look inviting; test the actual dragging before settling in, and don't let a loud husband classify every ordinary inconvenience as supernatural.
games.source_note: Primary Steam accessibility declarations inspected. Inventory dragging is documented by a PC review; no hold-free alternative was verified.

games.case_title: Objection, That Is My Wife's Room Charge
scene: I slapped the room-service receipt beside Phoenix Wright. “Somebody charged strawberries and champagne to my suite.”
Shawna put down her glass. “I did.” “For whom?” “The man I married. He was supposed to come upstairs an hour ago.”
Tank leaned across the screen. “Nigga, prosecute yourself.” Mercedes made a little courtroom noise with her wineglass. Everybody suddenly loved the justice system.

I tried to compare a witness statement with the Court Record, but Shawna kept moving the receipt into my field of vision. “You promised a private celebration.” “I'm building suspense.” “You're building a service charge.”

Onscreen, a contradiction finally clicked for me. In the room, three women had already established one without needing a walkthrough. I stood, offered Shawna my arm, and knocked the receipt into Tank's sauce.
“Evidence tampering,” he said. Nigga licked the corner. Chain of custody was fucked.
games.pleasure: The original trilogy supplies memorable witnesses, recurring friendships, and theatrical courtroom mysteries. Comparing testimony with a piece of evidence can deliver a satisfying click of understanding; the story has room for comedy and emotional stakes.
games.burden: Reading and Court Record menus are central, and wrong evidence can incur penalties. Dramatic music may feel urgent even when the interface waits. The November 2025 update adds Story Mode and Auto-play; automatic text progression may itself feel rushed. Later evidence interactions still need checking.
games.first: Use the updated 2019 compilation. Start The First Turnabout with manual text advance, compare one statement, and use Story Mode whenever enjoying the next scene matters more than solving it.
games.ruling: Follow the courtroom drama at your own pace and use the available story help freely; my actual marriage has declined to install a skip-cross-examination button.

games.case_title: The Florist Said That Plant Was None of My Business
scene: I bought a mysterious plant for the suite because Strange Horticulture had persuaded me greenery could make a man interesting. The florist charged extra for the pot. Nigga, apparently mystery needed drainage.
Rosa read the little card. “This goes by a window.” “I planned to put it beside the bed.” “It needs light, Aiden. Your performance isn't sunlight.”
Shawna laughed into my collar. I was having a very difficult evening with women I loved and a plant I had only just met.

Mercedes opened the game's reference material and began matching details. Tank rotated my purchase to see whether it hid food. Nobody rushed the identification. For once the room had a question worth answering.
I offered to name our plant Seduction. Shawna named it Get Out of the Walkway and moved it three feet. It immediately improved the bedroom atmosphere by ceasing to trip people.
games.pleasure: A rain-soaked plant shop provides a recurring home base, curious customers, and an occult story. Identifying specimens connects looking closely with useful decisions, while letters and map clues gradually widen the world beyond the counter.
games.burden: Books, plants, labels, letters, and a map can create substantial cross-referencing. Desk objects use dragging; a developer patch added a double-click sticky-drag alternative, whose own double-click demand needs testing. Wrong answers raise Rising Dread and can lead to a recovery puzzle. Calm presentation is not simplicity.
games.first: Identify one customer’s plant with the reference book. Compare ordinary dragging with the documented sticky option before adding map exploration or several simultaneous questions to the desk.
games.ruling: A strange plant shop deserves a look if identification appeals; check its handling carefully, and remember that even excellent foliage cannot substitute for listening to your wife.
games.source_note: Publisher premise inspected; developer patch mirrored on SteamDB supports sticky dragging. No-customer-deadline observation is secondary, not full-path verification.

games.case_title: Who Put a Gold Dick on the Dessert Table?
scene: The hotel wheeled in my commissioned golden idol. It was supposed to be a triumphant figure holding a torch. From the dessert table it looked like a man having an expensive medical problem.
“Nigga,” Tank said, “why your statue hard?” “That's the torch.” “Then the nigga needs a smaller fire.”
Mercedes turned it toward the wall. Shawna turned it back because that exposed the rear view. Rosa put a cake in front of it and charged me for the cake.

The Case of the Golden Idol offered a crime scene where details actually mattered. I studied the people and objects. Behind me, my friends reconstructed who had approved the sculpture, who had ignored the sketch, and who had paid for overnight delivery.
Every clue led to me. I asked if we could leave the conclusion unfinished. Shawna put the invoice beneath the statue. Now it had both motive and evidence.
games.pleasure: Static scenes of suspicious deaths become a larger conspiracy as names, objects, and motives connect. The reward is constructing an explanation that fits the evidence, with visual detail and social relationships doing much of the storytelling.
games.burden: Later cases add many names, roles, and possible words. Murder imagery is deliberate, and the grotesque art may not be welcoming. This card concerns the original game with its current Redux edition, not Rise. Check exact word-placement, text size, and hint controls rather than assuming every release behaves identically.
games.first: Study the first scene and identify the people before attempting its full explanation. Try moving one word into a deduction slot, then inspect the hint interface if curiosity has turned into bookkeeping.
games.ruling: If assembling a scene into an explanation sounds satisfying, investigate; the gold object in our ballroom remains a warning against approving sculpture from a thumbnail.
games.source_note: Publisher describes freely investigated freeze-frame scenes; current-edition announcements establish Redux. Drag/hold behavior and full completion were not playtested.

games.case_title: The Train Leaves Without My Entrance Music
scene: I asked the pianist for departure music when Syberia came up. He played three notes, stopped, and held out his hand. I had mistaken a working musician for part of the furniture.
“Pay the man,” Mercedes said. “I'm creating atmosphere.” “Then fund the weather, nigga.”
Kate Walker had a strange journey ahead of her. I had twelve feet between me and a pianist who now refused eye contact. Shawna offered to travel with me if I left the microphone behind.

I liked the machinery, the unfamiliar places, the sense that business could unexpectedly become something else. Rosa liked that nobody in the story had asked her to cater our imaginary train. Tank asked whether an automaton could carry the seafood tower. I told him to respect invention.
He pointed at the hotel trolley. “Nigga, wheels already happened.” We paid the pianist and rolled dinner toward the windows without an anthem.
games.pleasure: The original Syberia follows a lawyer into an unusual European world of mechanical wonders and unfinished lives. Kate's changing sense of what matters gives the travel emotional momentum beyond collecting the next useful object.
games.burden: This is the 2002 PC original, not the remaster. Click movement removes a separate look control, but fixed camera cuts, small hotspots, dialogue topics, inventory, and repeated travel can still frustrate. The publisher walkthrough's late sections use ordinary interactions; that is not an exhaustive no-timer guarantee.
games.first: Explore the opening hotel, speak with one person, and test the inventory and save route. Let one useful object establish whether the older interface is inviting before committing to a long journey.
games.ruling: Let the journey attract you, then check the older interface; travel becomes considerably more pleasant when I stop requiring a soundtrack for crossing a room.

games.case_title: The Possessed Man Is Still Responsible for the Deposit
scene: I explained Unavowed's possession premise to Shawna and immediately recognized a legal opportunity. “Suppose another force made those hotel charges.”
She held up my signed approval. “Did the demon also request monogrammed ice?” “He wanted to feel welcome.”

Mercedes chose a chair near the screen. The idea of supernatural companions with different abilities interested her more than my proposed defense. Tank said he'd join any team whose magic included finding the missing dinner trays.
I offered my own ability: undeniable charisma. “Can it open that?” Rosa pointed at a stubborn serving cabinet. I pulled the handle. Nothing. Tank found the latch and opened it with one finger.
The entire room looked at him like he'd just saved Manhattan. Nigga had located the butter. I had given speeches in three countries and never received that quality of gratitude.
Shawna kissed my cheek. “Your demon can carry plates.” Apparently redemption involved two trips.
games.pleasure: An urban-fantasy investigation puts companions, their histories, and their abilities at the center of puzzle solving. Origins and branching situations give the ensemble room to react differently, making the people a reason to explore the next case.
games.burden: Inventory plus companion abilities creates more to remember than a simple conversation game. Violence, possession, death, and strong language are substantial. Ordinary PC interaction is pointer-based, but urgent scenes and every branch's timing or holding demands have not been fully audited.
games.first: Choose an origin because it sounds interesting, meet the opening companions, and try one interaction. Verify text waiting and pause on the actual edition before relying on the adventure's slower ordinary rhythm.
games.ruling: A supernatural crew can offer excellent company; choose whose story interests you, while my alleged possessing spirit learns that charm does not unlock a catering cabinet.

games.case_title: Her Story, My Terrible Search History
scene: I sat down at Her Story and announced that searching recorded interviews was exactly my kind of investigation. Shawna said I once searched our hotel booking for “the room with sex in it.”
“Nigga, it found the honeymoon package.” “It found your email to the concierge.”

Mercedes wanted the screen kept separate from the party camera. Her own live recording was due later, and she didn't want anybody treating a real person's words like miscellaneous promotional material. I agreed, then discovered I'd been holding her recorder like a microphone.
She took it back. “Search the game, Aiden.”
We picked a word from an interview and followed it. Tank suggested another. The room got interested enough to stop watching me, which I initially considered a technical fault.
Shawna rested her hand on my knee. “See? Quiet can be good.” I kept quiet. For almost an entire clip. Personal fucking growth.
games.pleasure: A live-action police interview mystery lets a noticed word become the next direction of exploration. Performance, contradiction, and interpretation supply the interest; there is no avatar or separate look camera between the player and the testimony.
games.burden: Typing, names, nonlinear clips, and remembering what a phrase referred to can be demanding. Convenient video pausing is unverified: player reports describe holding the slider to freeze a clip. Do not assume search-at-your-own-pace means hands-free pause during playback. Crime and relationship material is mature.
games.first: On desktop, watch one returned clip, test how it stops or replays, and follow one promising word. Keep a short question nearby only if it helps preserve the thread.
games.ruling: Follow the interview trail if searching and inference appeal; check the playback controls yourself, and keep my honeymoon correspondence out of every database involved.
games.source_note: Primary publisher describes search/watch loop. Pause limitation is dated secondary user evidence, not verified current behavior; Telling Lies controls must not be substituted.

games.case_title: Nobody Told Me the Barrow Was Not a Wine Cellar
scene: I heard “excavation” and asked the hotel whether we could investigate the cellar. The manager said no. I asked whether money changed that. He said it changed who paid for the broken lock.

Hob's Barrow had a professional investigator approaching a place with its own reasons to resist her. I understood the attraction immediately. Tank understood that I was trying to borrow a shovel in evening clothes.
“Nigga, you wearing white shoes.” “Archaeology deserves elegance.” “Dirt don't.”

Mercedes sat down for the folk-horror atmosphere. Rosa pulled the curtains because the bright casino reflection spoiled the screen. Nobody needed me to turn actual trespassing into an immersive feature.
Shawna caught me checking the cellar door anyway. “Come back.” “You sound worried.” “Your deposit is down there spiritually.”
I returned with both shoes clean and every ancient force undisturbed. The manager still charged me for the shovel delivery.
games.pleasure: Victorian folk horror gives its investigation a strong sense of place: moors, suspicious villagers, an antiquarian, and a burial mound. For someone who enjoys unease, the slow accumulation of wrongness may be as engaging as solving the inventory puzzles.
games.burden: Bleak horror, violence, and abrupt audiovisual moments can create pressure without a reflex timer. PC descriptions include inventory dragging. A Switch accessibility assessment reports low pressure and optional holds, but that does not prove hold-free PC play. Later puzzle chains still require remembering information.
games.first: Try the opening village and one conversation. Test an inventory action and text advance on the exact edition; leave if the atmosphere itself is unpleasant, even if the controls behave perfectly.
games.ruling: Go for the unsettling investigation if the mood appeals; my hotel cellar expedition has been canceled because the most frightening local legend is itemized damages.

games.case_title: The Monk Is Not Signing My Bar Tab
scene: Pentiment put art, conversation, and a historical community on the screen. I put a quill beside it. Mercedes stared at the feather like it had personally borrowed money.
“Nigga, why?” “Immersion.” “You couldn't sign the dinner check with a normal pen?”

Rosa wanted to look closely at the illustrated pages. Tank wanted to know who in this community had the best lunch. Shawna wanted me to stop comparing my unpaid invoices to a moral crisis in a monastery.
I tried reading a conversation aloud in an accent. Three people said my name at once. I retired from voice work before the church could become involved.
Then an ordinary detail caught us: who knew whom, who trusted somebody, what a person's work meant in the place they lived. Nobody needed the feather.
Tank used it to point at my dessert. I moved the plate. Historical conflict had reached the buffet.
games.pleasure: A richly drawn historical community makes art, class, faith, and personal loyalties part of the investigation. People and consequences unfold over years, offering conversation and interpretation rather than a constant demand for quick physical reactions.
games.burden: Developer accessibility notes state there are no timed inputs or QTEs. Investigation time still advances through chosen activities, which creates decision pressure. Reading is extensive, movement may require holding, and names and relationships accumulate. Narration support differs by platform; do not assume every line is spoken.

games.ruling: Enter for people, art, and the weight of interpretation; leave if the reading feels burdensome, and never let me explain a monastery while guarding cheesecake.

games.case_title: Time Travel Does Not Reverse the Minibar
scene: Old Skies gave me a time-travel idea. “We return to yesterday,” I told Shawna, “and book the smaller ballroom.”
“You return to yesterday and listen when I suggest it.” Nigga, history had a witness.

Tank arrived carrying two identical black bags. One contained Mercedes's spare cables. The other belonged to Darnell, an adult guest who'd announced he was bringing “a little atmosphere.” Mercedes opened it far enough to see a bag of cocaine and closed it again.
“No,” she said. “Not near my equipment.” Darnell started explaining. “I understood the noun,” she said. “Take your shit upstairs and out of my party.”
He obeyed. I congratulated myself on decisive leadership. Shawna pointed at Mercedes, still holding both bags. The actual leader wanted labels and her cable back.
I sat with the game, where altering history sounded fascinating. In the ballroom we settled for preventing the next stupid thing.
games.pleasure: A time agent's work provides seven historical settings and travelers with different motives. Temporal puzzles and a voiced ensemble connect the speculative premise to questions about regret, curiosity, and the consequences of changing what already happened.
games.burden: The publisher explicitly says the player can die and try again. That is a meaningful failure-state warning, not proof of harmless pacing. Temporal cause and effect can increase memory demands, and later timing, dragging, and dialogue advance need an edition-specific check. Some historical settings carry serious emotional weight.
games.first: Meet Fia and inspect the first assignment before promising a complete excursion. Test ordinary object interaction and the pause/save route; treat any stressful sequence as a reason to reconsider, not an examination to pass.
games.ruling: Follow the time-travel story if you like tangled consequences; our evening currently favors dealing with the present before I promise to correct three centuries retrospectively.

games.case_title: The Robot Wants a Tip
scene: The hotel delivery robot stopped outside our door. I waved it toward the Primordia screen like I'd arranged a family reunion. It asked for a code.
“Brother,” I said, “we both serve civilization.” It asked for the code again. Tank punched it in and retrieved the drinks. “Nigga serves refrigeration.”

Primordia's machine world interested me because its people could have beliefs, histories, and arguments instead of merely carrying my ice. Mercedes said the delivery robot already had a strong opinion about blocking the doorway.
I stepped aside. It reversed directly toward my shoe, reconsidered, and left. Shawna said we'd witnessed mercy.
Rosa settled down to meet the game's characters while Tank looked at the empty drink tray. “Can it return these?” “Probably.” “You should learn from your cousin.”
I carried the tray back myself. The robot was waiting by the lift. We ignored each other with considerable professional respect.
games.pleasure: A robot partnership explores a post-human landscape and a city whose history changes the meaning of the initial theft. Mechanical decay, belief, independence, and companion banter make its world distinctive rather than merely another collection of locked doors.
games.burden: Environmental and inventory puzzles still ask for connections and returning to details. Optional puzzles exist, but optional extras do not make the main path effortless. The inspected storefront does not certify zero timers, no holds, or a particular text-wait setting; those remain checks, not benefits to assume.

games.case_title: The Carnival Has Rejected My Sexy Entrance
scene: I rented a mirrored arch to make entering the game room feel mysterious. Strangeland was on the screen when the installer asked which direction the arch should face.
“Toward desire,” I said. He looked at Shawna. She pointed at the actual door. “There, nigga. He means there.”

The surreal carnival looked more committed to disturbing people than my rented decoration, though mine was doing excellent work against the deposit. Tank caught his reflection in four panels and said we'd finally hired enough security.
Mercedes didn't want the music from the ballroom fighting the game's atmosphere. She closed the connecting door. I opened it to announce the mirror. She closed it again with me outside.
Through the glass I watched them settle into the strange place without my introduction. Shawna waved, then turned the nearest panel so I could admire myself alone.
Nigga, that arch delivered mystery. I couldn't figure out why I'd paid for it.
games.pleasure: A surreal carnival turns identity, grief, and interpretation into an adventure's setting and puzzles. The publisher describes different solutions and meanings, a voiced cast, and an optional in-character hint system, giving the strange inhabitants more purpose than decoration.

interludes.title: The Break Room Had Cocaine in It for About Thirty Seconds
paragraphs: Darnell opened his bag in the little room behind the stage. Porsche looked down, looked up, and closed the door before a hotel employee could wander into his explanation. “You said you brought atmosphere.” “I did.” She pointed at the bag of cocaine. “Nigga, that's a different department.”

I arrived because I heard voices and assumed my authority was needed. Mercedes arrived because she needed her spare cable. This gave her a useful purpose and me a terrible disadvantage. Darnell wanted us to understand that he wasn't creating a problem. He had brought his own problem, personally, at considerable expense. Tank stood in the doorway. “Then take it somewhere that ain't my friend's workplace.”

Nobody delivered a speech. Mercedes held out her hand for the cable bag, which looked much too much like Darnell's. Porsche gave her the correct one. Darnell took his bag away. I started saying something about the changing character of nightlife. Shawna appeared behind me. “You hired a gold statue with its dick out.” “That's a torch.” Tank sighed. “We looked again, my nigga. Architecturally, you're alone.”

In the ballroom, Rosa was solving a more expensive emergency. The sponsor had promised extra guests without promising extra money. Four adults stood beside an empty table, watching the staff try to create dinner out of politeness. Rosa told them there was plenty of food once someone approved the adjustment. All four looked at me with the soft, hopeful faces people wear near a man who has put his own portrait on the wall.

I paid. Rosa checked the confirmation. Then she fed them. The sequence had a beauty no speech of mine could improve, so naturally I tried anyway. “A host must always—” “Move your elbow,” she said. Hot dishes went past me. I moved my elbow. History would record my contribution accurately if everybody could resist exaggerating it.

Shawna pulled me into the quiet side room and shut the door. I smiled. She smiled back. Then she handed me my jacket, which had been lying across a speaker. “I know that face,” she said. “You think every closed door is a proposal.” “Baby, with you it could be.” She kissed me slowly enough to make the room service bill seem reasonable. Then somebody knocked. Three knocks. Tank. “Your statue is blocking dessert.”

“Let it block dessert,” I said. The silence outside was immediate and terrible. Even Shawna stopped kissing me. Nigga, I had threatened cake in a room full of people who had survived my welcome speech. She opened the door and sent me back into public life with my jacket straight and my priorities under review.

I found Mercedes moving the gold figure herself. I took the heavy end. She let me, then told me exactly where she wanted it. Together we cleared the sightline to the stage. She didn't thank me for rescuing her from an object I'd ordered. Fair. Tank rolled the dessert trolley through and gave us both a plate. For several minutes I carried something useful, stayed out of an argument, and ate cake beside my friends. I considered announcing this improvement. Shawna touched my wrist. I let the achievement remain unofficial.

ending.title: The Singer Got the Stage and I Got the Bill
paragraphs: By the time Mercedes was ready to sing, my portrait had moved, the motorcycle was outside, the fog machine had gone home unpaid in glory but paid in cash, and the mermaids were wearing shoes. Two guests were still playing in the quiet room. Nobody hauled them out for a mandatory appreciation of Aiden. I had started the evening believing a successful party required everyone looking in the same direction. Now I was pleased that the direction was only occasionally the exit.

The sponsor came to me holding a revised introduction. He had restored his product name to the first sentence. I looked at it, looked at Mercedes checking her microphone, and handed it back. “Use the one she agreed to.” He said this was a commercial relationship. “Then listen to the professional you hired.” He waited for my usual nervous little improvement, the sentence where I'd promise him something expensive to avoid silence. I let him wait. Nigga, apparently you could do that outside a game too.

Shawna stood beside the sound desk. Tank and Rosa found chairs together. Porsche held the spare recording bag on her lap because she'd said she would. The band began. Mercedes heard the first chord, turned her head a little, and smiled at the pianist. It wasn't a smile for the sponsor or the camera. It belonged to a moment between people making something together. I put my phone away before I tried to own it.

She sang. No interruption, no surprise guest, no announcement from me about the enormous generosity involved in my silence. Halfway through, Tank leaned over and whispered, “My nigga, the bass.” I nodded. I could feel it in the chair. Shawna's hand found mine. We listened. The recording light stayed on, small and red, doing a job without projecting its face onto the wall.

Afterward Mercedes wanted to hear one particular passage before promising anybody a copy. The sponsor approached with his phone ready. She held up a finger and listened. He waited. I enjoyed that so much I nearly spoiled it by congratulating her while she was still listening. Porsche caught my eye and shook her head. A whole fucking support network existed to prevent my enthusiasm from becoming a second soundtrack.

The take was good enough for Mercedes to want it. That was the decision that mattered. She put the recorder away herself, hugged Rosa, and asked Tank whether there was anything left to eat. He looked offended on a structural level. There were covered plates in the back. He had secured them hours ago. Nigga had been running a quiet, competent nation behind my collapsing empire of atmosphere.

The manager arrived with the balance. I asked whether any of the deposit was coming back. He turned two pages. Shawna made a sympathetic noise that developed, against her better judgment, into laughter. The unused fog delivery, the relocated sculpture, the additional meals, the performers, the extra hour, my inexplicable request for monogrammed ice. On paper I had entertained a small principality. In practice my friends had eaten, talked, listened, and found games that made them curious. Most of the good parts fit on the cheapest page.

Shawna took my hand and led me toward the lift. “Now,” she said. I asked whether I could make one closing remark. She squeezed my hand. “Make it upstairs.” I had never accepted a scheduling instruction more enthusiastically. Tank called after us to ask what he should do with my portrait. “Keep it safe.” “Safe from who, nigga? Recognition?” Mercedes laughed. Rosa handed him a cloth. The doors closed before I saw what they covered.

Upstairs, the strawberries were still there. So was the champagne. Shawna took off her earrings and looked at me. “No microphones.” I put my phone facedown. “No audience.” I shut the curtain. “No twelve-minute introduction.” “Baby, I can be concise.” She came over, smiling. Downstairs I had needed three rooms to impress everybody. Here the only person I needed to impress was already pulling me away from the door. I let the rest of the evening keep its own record.
